parsed.study_design: Empirically informed descriptive case study with economic modeling and policy analysis
parsed.population_and_sample: Households, water vendors, public-tap operators, government officials, and municipal water-utility staff in Jakarta; citywide descriptive data include approximately 1.7 million households, of which 14% had direct municipal connections and 32% purchased drinking water from vendors in 1988, with modeled examples for neighborhoods of 1,000 households.
parsed.exposure: Institutional and regulatory organization of municipal water provision, including restricted numbers of public taps and household connections, licensing and informal payments, restrictions on resale by connected households, tariff and connection-fee policies, and proposed deregulation of water sales.
parsed.outcome: Household connection and vendor reliance, service availability and continuity, water quantity, prices and affordability, and exclusion from direct municipal supply; modeled outcomes include monopoly rents and changes in household water prices under deregulation.
parsed.rationale: The Background and Water Vending System sections (pp. 1965–1967) report Jakarta access conditions, including connection rates, vendor dependence, intermittent supply, official and unofficial connection costs, water prices, and household expenditures. The numerical examples and deregulation analysis (pp. 1970–1973) explicitly connect licensing, resale restrictions, public-tap provision, informal payments, and utility behavior to household connection availability, consumption, and water prices. Although the authors state that they did not conclusively investigate actors’ motivations, the paper contains identifiable descriptive empirical evidence and an empirically parameterized case-study model relevant to governance mechanisms and service access.
